newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens says unscathed by Motorola.
newsitem.headline: Siemens says unscathed by Motorola.

text.p: German electronics giant Siemens AG said on Thursday it saw itself unscathed by the problems clawing at partner and competitor Motorola Inc.
Motorola's stock suffered on Wednesday after it said third-quarter earnings would be down sharply due to downturns in the semiconductor and mobile phone markets.
Motorola's problems "have nothing to do with us," said a spokesman for Siemens private communications networks division. "Mobile telephones are one of Siemens' most profitable businesses."
Output was increasing in terms of the number of telephones, and profit in the sector was rising, the spokesman said. He declined to give a specific profit forecast for the division.

A spokesman for Siemens' semiconductor division was equally sanguine. "We had foreseen the price drops that set in last December. The development of the market is now seen not as fast as before, but it's not so bad. We are flexible enough to change our plans if needed."
Siemens shares opened sharply lower in Frankfurt trading on Thursday but regained most of the ground by midday, down 12 pfennigs at 77.12 marks at 1030 GMT.
Private-sector analysts were a more cautious than Siemens, however.

Siemens semiconductor division, which made the biggest contribution to the company's profit last year, was likely to see a small decline this year, and could drop next year as much as 30 percent, said Hans-Peter Wodniok at Credit Lyonnais in London.
"But Siemens has a much bigger business than Motorola, and the impact of this will be diluted," Wodniok said.
Siemens is the largest European manufacturer of semiconductors, but Intel and Motorola of the U.S. have larger shares of the European market.
Siemens in the past year opened a new chip plant in Dresden, started construction on one in the U.K. and chose a site in Portugal that will add substantially to its semiconductor capacity.
It is also building a $1.5 billion plant in the U.S. together with Motorola.
The semiconductor division's investment programme has been under a normal review since mid-July, the spokesman said, but no decisions have been announced.
In July, Siemens said it would stick by its forecast of a 20 percent rise in profit for the year to September 30.
Profit dropped slightly in its semiconductor division in the nine months to June 30, but the components unit, which includes semiconductors, again made the biggest contribution to group earnings.
In the nine-month period, Siemens' semiconductor sales were up 13 percent to 3.4 billion marks ($2.25 billion), while new orders rose two percent to 3.8 billion marks.
Analysts said the structure of its chip business, its strong position in logic chips for the telecommunications and smart card industries would help offset some of the problems in the industry.

Some expected falling semiconductor prices to cut profit in Siemens division 17 percent in the year to September 30. While profit could fall again next year, Siemens was better positioned than many others in the industry.

Its cell-phone business was also going very well, they said. Sales of private communications systems, which includes mobile phones, rose 18 percent to 6.0 billion marks, while orders rose 21 percent ot 6.2 billion marks.
